summary:
At the Lunar South Pole, sun elevations never exceed ~1.5° above the horizon. A rover or lander resting on a sunlit crater rim can plunge into lethal darkness or lose direct-to-Earth communication simply by driving a few dozen meters. Existing exploration tools provide raw post-mission data, but require querying separate tables and spreadsheets to evaluate landing sites.

L-SPOC (Lunar South Pole Operations Console) solves this operational challenge by unifying 3D terrain dynamics, orbital mechanics, power budgets, and comms into a single real-time console. 

Powered by NASA LRO LOLA 20-meter elevation models and JPL Horizons DE440 ephemerides, L-SPOC precomputes multi-height horizon elevation masks. This enables operators, flight controllers, and scientists to compute solar disc occlusion, line-of-sight to Deep Space Network stations, 2-year survival windows, and autonomous obstacle-avoidance escape routes in O(1) time at 60 FPS on any browser without heavy workstations.
details:
1. What It Does & How It Works

Planning surface exploration at the Lunar South Pole requires solving two existential threats: low-angle solar terrain shadowing (sun elevations never exceed ~1.5°) and direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication occultation by crater rims. A rover or habitat resting on a sunlit ridge can plunge into lethal darkness or lose line-of-sight to Earth by traversing just a few dozen meters.

L-SPOC (Lunar South Pole Operations Console) bridges the gap between post-mission GIS analysis and real-time flight operations by integrating:

  • High-Resolution NASA Data Pipeline: Built upon NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) LOLA 20-meter digital elevation models (DEM) and JPL Horizons DE440 high-precision ephemerides.
  • Precomputed Horizon Occlusion Engine: High-fidelity 3D raycasting over 40 km terrain at 20 m resolution is computationally prohibitive for client browsers. We precomputed 64-azimuth topocentric horizon elevation masks across three observer heights (0 m ground, 2 m rover deck, 10 m mast/lander antenna). This allows L-SPOC to compute exact solar disc occlusion and Earth line-of-sight in O(1) mathematical time at 60 FPS on standard consumer hardware.
  • Two-Year Survival Window Ribbon: A continuous timeline calculating operational survival classes (Sun+Comm, Solar Only, Comm Only, Night) for every hour from 2026 through 2027, highlighting longest continuous darkness periods to prevent battery depletion.
  • Autonomous GNC & Sortie Planning: Real-time pathfinding algorithms compute safe traverse corridors that adhere to a 15° nominal / 20° maximum slope threshold, avoid permanently shadowed regions (PSRs), and dynamically plan escape routes to sunlit havens as shadow fronts move.
  • First-Person MastCam Viewport: A 4-meter mast camera simulator with 2-axis pan/tilt telemetry, pitch/roll crosshairs, and multispectral science filters (including 950nm NIR for identifying volatile ice deposits).

2. Benefits & Creative Innovations

  • Instant Scenario Comparison vs. Multi-Tool Fragmentation: Instead of querying separate ephemeris tables in JPL Horizons, manually projecting angles onto DEMs in Moon Trek, and cross-referencing spreadsheets, operators can test landing sites and launch windows in seconds with instant visual feedback.
  • Lommel-Seeliger Photometric Regolith Shader: Unlike generic 3D viewers that use Lambertian shading, our WebGL shaders implement authentic lunar regolith scattering, capturing the extreme contrast of airless lunar shadows, the lunar opposition surge, and subtle earthshine in shadowed crater rims.
  • Space Weather & DSN Telemetry Integration: Free-space path loss (FSPL), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and one-way light time latency are calculated across all three Deep Space Network complexes (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra). NASA DONKI integration correlates real-time coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and geomagnetic storms to alert operators of S-band scintillation risks.

3. Factors Considered

  • Moon-Me-In-Earth Frame Mechanics: Correctly accounted for the Moon’s orbital eccentricity and the ±7° optical and physical libration of the Earth in the lunar sky, which causes the Earth to drift above and below crater horizons over the 27.3-day sidereal month.
  • Airless Radiative Environment: Because the Moon lacks an atmosphere, twilight does not exist; shadow boundaries are razor-sharp. Our lighting model accurately transitions from full solar irradiance to total pitch black across sub-meter distances.
  • Mechanical Rover Limitations: Rover traversability was modeled using real-world Artemis-class and VIPER specifications, including wheel ground clearance, motor power draw under variable slope angles, and battery thermal survival margins during lunar night.

4. Intended Impact

  • For Mission Architects & Flight Controllers: Enables rapid "what-if" trade-off evaluations when launch dates slip or lander targeting coordinates adjust.
  • For Science & Engineering Teams: Bridges the communication gap between planetary scientists seeking volatile samples in deep, permanently shadowed cold traps and power engineers demanding continuous solar illumination and DTE telemetry.
  • For Public Engagement & Education: Translates complex celestial mechanics, ephemeris calculations, and lunar topography into an intuitive, gamified simulation that communicates the harsh realities of lunar exploration.

5. Tools, Coding Languages & Technologies

  • Front-End Framework: TypeScript, React 19, Next.js (App Router), Tailwind CSS.
  • 3D Graphics & Shaders: Three.js, React Three Fiber (R3F), custom WebGL GLSL fragment/vertex shaders.
  • Ephemeris & Scientific Computations: JPL Horizons DE440 Chebyshev polynomial evaluations, selenographic coordinate transformations, and binary elevation format parsers.
  • Verification & Testing: Vitest automated test suite (83 unit tests verifying topocentric coordinate conversions, solar power math, horizon raycasting, and libration bounds against published NASA data).
